title: How Penicillin Changed Modern Medicine
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Long ago, people used mould to treat infections. Many cultures knew that fungi could help heal sick bodies. However, they did not know the exact parts that stopped the sickness. In 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming made a big discovery in London.
pages.caption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

imageProvenance.credit: Science Museum London / Science and Society Picture Library

evidence.fileTitle: File:Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod, 1935 (9672239344).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

pages.text: Fleming left some culture plates on his lab table before a holiday. When he came back, he saw a strange blue-green mould growing on one plate. He noticed that bacteria did not grow near the mould. The mould was killing the bad bacteria around it.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

evidence.fileTitle: File:Synthetic Production of Penicillin TR1468.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

pages.text: Fleming named this new antibacterial substance "penicillin". He tested it on different bacteria and found it could kill some types. But Fleming could not isolate the pure chemical compound because he lacked strong training in chemistry, and his work stopped.

Years later, in 1939, a group of scientists at Oxford University started researching penicillin again. Led by Howard Florey, the team figured out how to grow the mould well. They also extracted, purified, and stored the penicillin safely in their laboratory.

The team tested penicillin on animals to check if it was safe. Soon, the United States helped produce large amounts of the medicine. Penicillin saved thousands of soldiers during the Second World War. Fleming, Florey, and Chain won a Nobel Prize in 1945.
pages.caption: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine medal awarded to Sir Alexander Fleming, on display at the National Museum of Scotland

evidence.fileTitle: File:Nobel prize medal for medicine, Sweden, 1945, to Sir Alexander Fleming (1881-1955) who discovered Penicillin. On display at the National Museum of Scotland.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine medal awarded to Sir Alexander Fleming, on display at the National Museum of Scotland

pages.text: Long before modern laboratories existed, ancient societies across the world used moulds to treat infections. Although these traditional treatments often worked because many fungi naturally produce antibiotics, ancient practitioners could never precisely identify or isolate the active components responsible for the healing properties.
pages.caption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

imageProvenance.credit: Science Museum London / Science and Society Picture Library

evidence.fileTitle: File:Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod, 1935 (9672239344).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

pages.text: A major turning point occurred in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London. Scottish physician Alexander Fleming left several culture plates of bacteria on his laboratory bench before taking a holiday. Upon his return, he noticed that a contaminant blue-green mould had grown and killed nearby bacteria.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

evidence.fileTitle: File:Synthetic Production of Penicillin TR1468.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

pages.text: Fleming named the antibacterial substance "penicillin" and demonstrated that it could kill specific harmful bacteria. Yet, because he lacked advanced chemical training, his attempts to isolate the pure compound failed. Consequently, work on penicillin at St Mary's ended by 1929, and his initial publication received little attention.

Ten years later, in 1939, a dedicated team of scientists at the University of Oxford led by Howard Florey resumed the research. Using Fleming's original paper and a mould sample, they devised methods for cultivating the mould, purifying the extract, and measuring its purity with new assays.

After successful animal safety tests, the private sector and agricultural departments developed mass production techniques. Penicillin became vital during the Second World War, saving thousands of soldiers. In 1945, Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their monumental discovery and development.
pages.caption: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine medal awarded to Sir Alexander Fleming, on display at the National Museum of Scotland

evidence.fileTitle: File:Nobel prize medal for medicine, Sweden, 1945, to Sir Alexander Fleming (1881-1955) who discovered Penicillin. On display at the National Museum of Scotland.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine medal awarded to Sir Alexander Fleming, on display at the National Museum of Scotland

pages.text: While ancient cultures globally exploited the empirical properties of fungi to combat infections, early practitioners remained inherently incapable of isolating active antimicrobial constituents. The foundational breakthrough materialized in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital, where Alexander Fleming experimentally verified that a contaminating Penicillium mould secreted a distinct antibacterial agent.
pages.caption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

imageProvenance.credit: Science Museum London / Science and Society Picture Library

evidence.fileTitle: File:Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod, 1935 (9672239344).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sample of penicillin mould presented by Alexander Fleming to Douglas Macleod in 1935

pages.text: Fleming's serendipitous discovery relied on precise environmental conditions during his absence, which favoured initial mould proliferation followed by bacterial growth. Upon returning, he observed zones of inhibition surrounding the mould colony, leading him to coin the term "penicillin" for the active broth filtrate that selectively eradicated specific Gram-positive pathogens.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

evidence.fileTitle: File:Synthetic Production of Penicillin TR1468.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, 1943

pages.text: Despite initial demonstrations, academic reception proved indifferent. Furthermore, because Fleming lacked formal biochemical training and subsequent collaborative efforts stalled in purifying the compound, primary research at St Mary's effectively ceased by 1929, leaving the therapeutic potential largely dormant for a decade.

The trajectory shifted radically in 1939 when Howard Florey spearheaded an Oxford research team to systematically reinvestigate penicillin. They engineered robust cultivation protocols, established purification and freeze-drying methodologies, and formulated reliable assays to quantify substance purity prior to conducting rigorous animal safety and efficacy trials.

Facilitated by agricultural scaling and industrial manufacturing techniques, penicillin transformed Allied military healthcare during the Second World War, preserving countless lives. In recognition of this monumental translational achievement, Fleming, Florey, and Ernst Chain jointly received the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: The History and Preservation of Palestinian Place Names
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The place names of Palestine have a very long history. Many names come from ancient Canaanite, Hebrew, and Aramaic languages. Over thousands of years, successive empires ruled the region. Each group left marks on how places are named, creating a rich history that people still study today.
pages.caption: In 1639, Thomas Fuller's The Historie of the Holy Warre included "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine", comparing the historical names of key Biblical locations. Several of the names for "today" are incorrect and show a lack of familiarity with Arabic names and orthography

evidence.fileTitle: File:Thomas Fuller, 1639, The Historie of the Holy Warre, Chapter I page 38, "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine".jpg
evidence.articleCaption: In 1639, Thomas Fuller's The Historie of the Holy Warre included "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine", comparing the historical names of key Biblical locations. Several of the names for "today" are incorrect and show a lack of familiarity with Arabic names and orthography

pages.text: Most place names in the region share Semitic roots. Very few names come from Greek or Turkish origins. Local populations used languages like Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic for thousands of years. Even when rulers changed, people often kept using the old names for their towns and fields.

Many names describe physical features of the land, such as water sources. For example, words for wells and springs appear in both Hebrew and Arabic place names. Beersheba and Bir as 'Saba both relate to wells, while En Gedi and 'Ayn Jeddi refer to natural water springs.

For a long time, researchers did not realize how well local people preserved ancient names. In the late 19th century, British groups began asking local farmers about place names. These farmers helped match modern Arabic names to ancient historical and archaeological sites.

Place names are also important for family history. Many Palestinian families use their village names as surnames. This tradition connects people to their places of origin. Today, place names remain a subject of deep scholarship and discussions about history and identity.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Preservation of Palestinian Place Names

pages.text: Place names in Palestine reflect thousands of years of cultural exchange and successive imperial rulers. Most modern names are Arabized forms of ancient Canaanite, Biblical Hebrew, or Aramaic terms. Although these names have survived for millennia, their original meanings were often understood by only a few people.
pages.caption: In 1639, Thomas Fuller's The Historie of the Holy Warre included "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine", comparing the historical names of key Biblical locations. Several of the names for "today" are incorrect and show a lack of familiarity with Arabic names and orthography

pages.text: Almost all regional place names share Semitic roots, with Latin influences appearing rarely and Greek or Turkish origins almost non-existent. Despite modifications introduced by classical ruling elites, the local population maintained the underlying Semitic naming traditions across generations.

Toponymic continuity is strongly linked to the physical environment. Aharoni noted that many names survived with remarkable consistency because they reflected enduring agricultural features. Terms for water sources, such as 'be'er' in Hebrew and 'bir' in Arabic for wells, or 'en' and ''ayn' for springs, appear frequently.

In the late 19th century, the Palestine Exploration Fund recognized the importance of geographical naming. British Mandatory authorities subsequently gathered information from local fellahin, whose oral knowledge helped identify ancient archaeological sites. Scholars like Edward Robinson also used linguistic analysis of Arabic place names to uncover biblical locations.

Family naming customs also reflect this geography. Since past centuries, Palestinians have adopted village names as surnames, a practice visible in modern telephone directories. Since the establishment of Israel, thousands of place names have also been Hebraized, making place names a subject of contention tied to historical claims.

C1-C2.headline: Toponymic Continuity and Stratigraphy in Palestine

pages.text: The nomenclature of Palestine encapsulates a multilayered history shaped by successive imperial administrations. The prevailing topographic designations primarily represent Arabized adaptations of ancient Canaanite, Biblical Hebrew, and Aramaic terms transmitted across millennia, preserving linguistic strata largely opaque to casual observers.
pages.caption: In 1639, Thomas Fuller's The Historie of the Holy Warre included "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine", comparing the historical names of key Biblical locations. Several of the names for "today" are incorrect and show a lack of familiarity with Arabic names and orthography

evidence.fileTitle: File:Thomas Fuller, 1639, The Historie of the Holy Warre, Chapter I page 38, "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine".jpg
evidence.articleCaption: In 1639, Thomas Fuller's The Historie of the Holy Warre included "A table shewing the varietie of place names in Palestine", comparing the historical names of key Biblical locations. Several of the names for "today" are incorrect and show a lack of familiarity with Arabic names and orthography

pages.text: Linguistic analysis reveals an overwhelming preponderance of Semitic roots, with negligible Greek or Turkish inputs and scarce Latin contributions. While classical antiquity introduced modifications driven by administrative elites, the underlying Semitic nomenclature persisted due to uninterrupted speech communities in the southern Levant.

Scholars such as Yohanan Aharoni documented exceptional pre-modern name preservation along the Eastern Mediterranean highland chain. This remarkable continuity is attributed to a shared Semitic linguistic background and the tendency of toponyms to reflect extant agricultural features, including hydrographic elements like springs and cisterns.

Systematic geographical inquiry began in the late 19th century when the Palestine Exploration Fund and British Mandatory authorities consulted local fellahin. These agrarian communities preserved authentic ancient nomenclature, enabling researchers to correlate modern toponyms with biblical and historical archaeological sites.

Beyond cartography, toponyms permeated social structures through the adoption of nisba surnames derived from villages, a custom documented across centuries. In contemporary contexts, place names remain heavily contested, intersecting with cartographic and archaeological proofs used to validate competing historical claims.

title: The History of the Armillary Sphere
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: An armillary sphere is a special model of the sky. It has a round frame made of metal rings. These rings show lines in the sky and important paths like the sun's path. It is very different from a simple globe that only shows the stars.
pages.caption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

imageProvenance.credit: physical object: Jost Bürgi, Antonius EisenhoitPhotograph: Chris Bainbridge

evidence.fileTitle: File:Armillary sphere with astronomical clock.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

pages.text: People invented this tool a long time ago. Ancient China and ancient Greece both made armillary spheres long before modern times. Later, scientists in the Islamic world and medieval Europe also built and used them to study the stars and planets.

In India, astronomers used these spheres for early observations. Famous texts describe how they worked. Indian scholars used systems based on the equator, while Greek versions used different sky coordinates. They helped calculate star positions carefully.
pages.caption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ptolemy 1476 with armillary sphere model.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

pages.text: Countries also used the sphere as an important symbol. Portugal put the armillary sphere on flags and coats of arms during the Age of Discovery. King Manuel I used it as his personal symbol, and it appears in old art today.
pages.caption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

evidence.fileTitle: File:6' Armillary Sphere @ San Jacinto Battle Field, Texas.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

pages.text: Today, people still see armillary spheres in interesting places. A large metal sculpture of one stands in a big airport. Another artistic model helps light the special Paralympic heritage flame at Stoke Mandeville Stadium in the United Kingdom.

B1-B2.headline: The History of the Armillary Sphere

pages.text: An armillary sphere is a mechanical model of the celestial sphere. It consists of a framework of graduated metal rings that represent important astronomical features, such as celestial coordinates and the ecliptic. Unlike a standard celestial globe, which maps constellations on a smooth surface, an armillary sphere uses rings to demonstrate the motion of objects in the sky.
pages.caption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

imageProvenance.credit: physical object: Jost Bürgi, Antonius EisenhoitPhotograph: Chris Bainbridge

evidence.fileTitle: File:Armillary sphere with astronomical clock.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

pages.text: Historical records show that the device was invented separately in ancient China, possibly by the fourth century BC, and in ancient Greece during the third century BC. When Earth sits at the center, it is called a geocentric model, whereas placing the Sun at the center creates a Copernican model.

Astronomers across different cultures refined the instrument over centuries. Islamic scholars like Ibrahim al-Fazari and Abbas Ibn Firnas built improved models, and Persian astronomers later described spherical astrolabes. In Korea, inventor Chang Yŏngsil constructed a famous armillary sphere named Honcheonui in 1433 by order of King Sejong.
pages.caption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ptolemy 1476 with armillary sphere model.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

pages.text: Before the invention of the European telescope, the armillary sphere served as the primary instrument for determining celestial positions. Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe constructed three massive armillary spheres to make exceptionally precise measurements of stars and planets, detailing his work in his published astronomical mechanics.
pages.caption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

evidence.fileTitle: File:6' Armillary Sphere @ San Jacinto Battle Field, Texas.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

pages.text: Beyond science, the sphere holds deep cultural and national significance. Portugal famously associated the device with its Age of Discovery, featuring it prominently in heraldry and on the national flag. Modern variations also appear as major public sculptures and even in ceremonies honoring the Paralympic Movement.

C1-C2.headline: Evolution and Legacy of the Armillary Sphere

pages.text: The armillary sphere functions as a sophisticated three-dimensional model of celestial coordinates, utilizing an interconnected skeletal framework of metal rings to delineate astronomical circles such as the ecliptic and celestial meridians. This structural configuration distinguishes it fundamentally from solid celestial globes designed primarily for mapping constellation cartography.
pages.caption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

imageProvenance.credit: physical object: Jost Bürgi, Antonius EisenhoitPhotograph: Chris Bainbridge

evidence.fileTitle: File:Armillary sphere with astronomical clock.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Jost Bürgi and Antonius Eisenhoit: Armillary sphere with astronomical clock, made in 1585 in Kassel, now at Nordiska Museet in Stockholm

pages.text: Historical attribution indicates independent invention in ancient China by the fourth century BC and in ancient Greece during the third century BC. Depending on the designated center, the apparatus operates as either a geocentric configuration or a heliocentric Copernican model, demonstrating apparent stellar movement relative to the observer.

Cross-cultural refinement characterized its medieval trajectory. Islamic astronomers advanced its construction, while Indian treatises documented equatorial coordinate adaptations that contrasted with Greek ecliptical models. In East Asia, Korean artisans like Chang Yŏngsil engineered complex instruments such as the Honcheonui under royal directives.
pages.caption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

evidence.fileTitle: File:Ptolemy 1476 with armillary sphere model.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Ptolemy with an armillary sphere model, by Joos van Ghent and Pedro Berruguete, 1476, Louvre, Paris

pages.text: Prior to the seventeenth-century adoption of the telescope, the armillary sphere remained the premier observational instrument for fixing celestial positions. Tycho Brahe elevated its precision to unprecedented levels, constructing gargantuan metallic rings that enabled remarkably accurate empirical tracking of planetary and stellar trajectories.
pages.caption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

evidence.fileTitle: File:6' Armillary Sphere @ San Jacinto Battle Field, Texas.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 6' Armillary Sphere at the San Jacinto Battle Field in La Porte, Texas

pages.text: Culturally, the instrument transcended pure science to become an enduring emblem of exploration. Quintessentially linked to Portuguese maritime expansion during the Age of Discovery, the armillary sphere permeates national heraldry, monumental airport exhibits, and contemporary ceremonial traditions such as the Paralympic heritage flame.

Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe constructed three massive armillary spheres to make exceptionally precise measurements of stars and planets, detailing his work in his published astronomical mechanics.

pages.text: Beyond science, the sphere holds deep cultural and national significance. Portugal famously associated the device with its Age of Discovery, featuring it prominently in heraldry and on the national flag. Modern variations also appear as major public sculptures and even in ceremonies honoring the Paralympic Movement.
